newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian coffee prices firming up on global demand.
newsitem.headline: Indian coffee prices firming up on global demand.

text.p: India's domestic coffee prices are firming up after a dip in coffee output and a favourable global market, exporters and planters said on Monday.

"Coffee powder prices rose by ten rupees per kg on February 23 and by another 10 rupees on Monday. It is expected to rise by another ten rupees before March-end," said A.P. Jayakumar, secretary of the All India Coffee Merchants Association (AICMA).
"That will make the price 180 rupees per kg," Jayakumar said.
AICMA sets the retail prices for domestic coffee powder.
Traders said coffee powder was priced at 160 rupees per kg at this time last year. The prices touched a peak of 180 rupees per kg in 1995 following a crop failure in Brazil.
AICMA president R.P. Sarathy said Arabica grade coffee, consumed in large proportions, was in short supply.

"Of the 80,000 tonnes (of Srabica) expected to be produced this year, 47,500 tonnes have already been contracted for exports by exporters and growers," he said. "By June-July there will be a severe crunch."
Growers are keen to export taking advantage of a favourable global market.
The U. S. State Department has estimated coffee production in 1996/97 (October-September) at 97 million bags of 60 kg each against a consumption of 99 million bags.
"This will keep the world prices high in the coming months. Exporters have already contracted till May," said Appaya (one name) a planter.
Sarathy said domestic traders did not have stocks and growers were selling to them at high prices. "So we are left with no option but to raise the prices in the retail market."
Planters said a fall in ouput had also contributed to the shortage in the domestic market.
Planters and officials differed on the coffee output in 1996/97.
"The output in 1996/97 season will not exceed 190,000 tonnes, " said I.J.J. Rebello, chairman of the coffee committee of the United Planters Association of Southern India (UPASI).
Jayakumar said the crop would be only around 180,000 tonnes.
"We will have a crop of around 205,000 tonnes comprising 89,950 tonnes of arabica and 115,000 tonnes of robusta," said an official of the state-run Coffee Board.
The board had in May estimated the 1996/97 output at 219,000 tonnes but scaled it down to 205,000 tonnes in November.
India produced 200,000 tonnes of coffee in 1995/96, comprising 95,000 tonnes Arabica and 105,000 tonnes Robusta.
